processing: The flowering tops are cut as the blossoms open and dried, then infused; no other processing.
harvest_season: Flowering tops are taken from bud to full flower, within the June to August bloom.
appearance_dry: Cut yellow-green stems and small leaves with dried golden-brown flower pieces.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden to amber-red, deepening with time.
appearance_wet: Soft olive-brown leaf and stem pieces with darkened flowers.
taste_profile: Herbal and somewhat bitter, with a slight pungency and a hint of sweetness.

brewing.notes: About 1 to 2 teaspoons per cup, steeped for 10 minutes. Check with a doctor first if you take any prescription medicine: it speeds up the breakdown of many drugs.

vintage_note: Sold by no vintage, usually as cut flowering tops or in teabags from pharmacies and herb shops. As with other dried herbs, this year's harvest is best; look for visible flower pieces rather than mostly stem.
description:
St John's wort tea is an infusion of the flowering tops of Hypericum perforatum, a golden-flowered perennial common on dry meadows and forest edges. In Russian it is zveroboy.

Timing matters in the making. The tops are taken around flowering and then dried, since the balance of compounds shifts with the stage of harvest.

The cup is plainly herbal and a little bitter, with some sweetness behind it. A 10-minute covered steep is usual.

This is the herb on this shelf that most deserves respect. It makes the body clear many medicines faster, including contraceptive pills, antidepressants, anticoagulants, immunosuppressants and antiretrovirals, and it can increase sensitivity to sunlight. It is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
history:
The plant has a long history in European folk medicine, reflected in Russian names such as zayachya krov (hare's blood) and krovavets. Little is documented about the tea as a distinct drink, beyond its steady place in household herb collections.

Its modern reputation rests on two things: its use for low mood and the later recognition that it interferes with many prescription medicines.
